lessons.title: How Companies Raise Money from Markets: IPOs, QIPs and Rights Issues

children.text: This is the primary market in action. When your company announces an IPO, a QIP or a rights issue, the finance team suddenly gets very busy and everyone else guesses at what it means. This lesson explains each route, who is allowed to participate, and what it does to the shares you already hold.

body.text: Raising equity is selling a slice of ownership for cash. The company gets money it never has to repay, and existing shareholders get a smaller share of a bigger business. Whether that is a good trade depends entirely on what the money buys.

children.text: The Five Routes to Raising Equity

body.caption: How Indian Companies Raise Equity

body.text: The distinction that trips up almost everyone: in a fresh issue, new shares are created and the company receives the cash. In an offer for sale, existing shares simply change hands and the money goes to the selling shareholder, often a promoter or an early investor. Most Indian IPOs are a mix of both, and the prospectus states exactly how much is which.

body.title: Follow the Money
body.question: A company's ₹2,000 crore IPO is made up of a ₹700 crore fresh issue and a ₹1,300 crore offer for sale by early investors. How much does the company receive to fund its business?
options: Nothing, since the shares were already issued
body.explanation: Only the fresh issue portion of ₹700 crore reaches the company. The ₹1,300 crore goes to the early investors selling their stakes, which is a perfectly legitimate exit route but funds nothing inside the business. Always check this split before assuming an IPO means expansion.

body.title: Why a Company Might Pick Equity Over Debt

columns.label: Raising Equity
points: No repayment obligation and no fixed interest
Nothing to service if the business has a bad year
Existing shareholders are diluted and give up part of future profits
New shareholders get voting rights and a say in governance
Expensive in the long run if the business does very well

columns.label: Raising Debt
points: Principal and interest must be paid whatever happens
A missed payment can trigger default and enforcement
No ownership is given up and no votes are handed out
Interest is tax deductible, which lowers the effective cost
Cheaper if the business earns more than the interest rate

children.text: Inside an IPO, Step by Step

body.title: From Board Approval to Listing Day

events.title: Board and Shareholder Approval
events.description: The company decides to go public, appoints merchant bankers, and gets internal approvals in place.

events.title: DRHP Filed With SEBI
events.description: The draft red herring prospectus is filed. It discloses the business, financials, litigation, promoter holdings, risk factors and what the money will be used for.

events.title: SEBI Observations
events.description: SEBI reviews the draft and issues observations. The company must address them before proceeding. SEBI checks disclosure, and does not certify that the issue is fairly priced.

events.title: RHP With Price Band
events.description: The red herring prospectus is filed with a price band and issue dates. The final price is discovered through bidding, within that band.

events.title: Anchor Book
events.description: Large institutional investors are allotted shares a day before the issue opens, with a lock-in period. Their participation is publicly disclosed and is read as a signal of institutional appetite.

events.title: The Issue Opens
events.description: Investors bid during a short window, usually three working days. Retail applications go through ASBA, so the money is blocked in your bank account rather than debited.

events.title: Basis of Allotment
events.description: If the issue is oversubscribed, retail allotment is decided by lottery on the minimum lot. Blocked funds are released for unsuccessful applicants.

events.title: Listing
events.description: The shares start trading on NSE and BSE. Indian rules have compressed this to a short, fixed timeline after the issue closes, far faster than most global markets.

stats.label: Qualified Institutional Buyers
stats.context: Of a standard book-built issue, for an eligible company

stats.label: Retail Investors
stats.context: Reserved portion, allotted by lottery when oversubscribed

body.text: A loss-making or short-track-record company can still list, but then a much larger share of the issue must go to institutional buyers and the retail portion shrinks sharply. If you see an unusually small retail quota, that is the rulebook telling you something about the company's financial history. Read the risk factors before the price band.

children.text: QIP: The Fast Lane for Listed Companies

markDefs.definition: Qualified Institutions Placement: a route allowing an already listed company to issue fresh shares to qualified institutional buyers such as mutual funds, insurers and banks, without the time and paperwork of a full public issue.
Qualified Institutional Buyer: a category of large, regulated investors, including mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds, banks and foreign portfolio investors.

children.text: A
QIP
lets a listed company raise large sums in days rather than months, by selling fresh shares only to
qualified institutional buyers

. SEBI rules set a floor price linked to recent market prices, so the company cannot issue shares cheaply to favoured parties. As an employee shareholder you cannot participate, and your stake gets diluted, but the company gets capital quickly and without taking on debt.

body.label: Why Companies Love QIPs
body.context: No lengthy public issue process, no retail marketing, and pricing anchored to recent market prices. This is why QIP announcements cluster when markets are strong.

children.text: Rights Issue: The One Where You Are Invited

A rights issue offers new shares to existing shareholders only, in proportion to what they already own, usually at a price below the market price. That discount looks like free money. It is not, and the arithmetic shows why.
Take an employee shareholder holding 400 shares of a company trading at ₹300. The company announces a 1:4 rights issue at ₹200, meaning one new share for every four held.

stats.label: Rights Entitlement
stats.context: One for every four held, at ₹200 each

body.latex: \text{TERP} = \frac{(\text{Old Shares} \times \text{Market Price}) + (\text{New Shares} \times \text{Rights Price})}{\text{Total Shares After Issue}}
body.caption: The theoretical ex-rights price: where the share should trade once the discounted new shares exist.

children.text: Putting the numbers in: (400 × ₹300 + 100 × ₹200) ÷ 500 = ₹1,40,000 ÷ 500 = ₹280 per share. The price drifts from ₹300 towards ₹280 not because anything went wrong, but because more shares now exist. The shareholder who paid ₹20,000 is no better or worse off in theory. The shareholder who ignored the offer is genuinely worse off, because the price adjusted downwards and they got nothing in return.

body.text: If you cannot or do not want to put in more money, rights entitlements can usually be sold on the exchange during the offer period, since Indian rights issues now trade entitlements electronically. Doing nothing at all is the one option that guarantees you lose value.

body.title: Your Rights Entitlement
body.prompt: You hold 600 shares. The company announces a 1:4 rights issue at ₹200 per share. If you take up your full entitlement, how much cash do you need to pay, in ₹?
body.explanation: 600 ÷ 4 = 150 new shares. 150 × ₹200 = ₹30,000. After the issue you would hold 750 shares. Note that entitlement is always a ratio of what you already own, which is exactly what makes a rights issue non-dilutive for shareholders who participate in full.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: In an IPO, retail application money is not debited immediately but blocked in your bank account under the mechanism called ___.
body.explanation: ASBA stands for Application Supported by Blocked Amount. Your money stays in your account, earning interest, until shares are allotted. If you get no allotment, the block is simply released.

body.title: What Dilution Actually Does to Your ESOPs

children.text: Dilution means your shares become a smaller percentage of a larger company. Whether that hurts depends on what the company does with the money:
Good dilution.
The company raises ₹500 crore, builds capacity that lifts profits by more than the extra shares dilute them, and earnings per share eventually rises. Your smaller percentage is worth more in rupees.
Bad dilution.
The company raises money to repay debt taken for a failed project, profits do not improve, and earnings per share falls permanently because it is now divided across more shares.
For option holders specifically.
Your exercise price does not change when the company issues fresh shares, so what matters to you is the share price after the raise, and whether the capital makes the business more valuable.
The question to ask at a town hall is never "are we diluting?" but "what does this capital buy, and when does it start earning more than it costs?"

body.title: The Monday Morning QIP Announcement
body.scenario: Your listed employer announces a ₹1,500 crore QIP to fund a new manufacturing plant. The stock dips about 3% on the news. A colleague with vested ESOPs sends you a message: "They are printing new shares and mine are worth less. Should I sell before it drops more?"
body.prompt: How do you respond, staying within what an employee can responsibly say?
body.modelAnswer: Separate the mechanics from the judgement. Mechanically, a QIP does create new shares, so each existing share represents a slightly smaller slice of the company, and the shares are issued to institutions at a price linked to recent market levels, which is why the stock often dips on announcement. That is dilution, and it is real. The judgement part is what the ₹1,500 crore buys: if the new plant earns more than the cost of that capital, profits grow faster than the share count and shareholders end up better off, which is the whole argument for raising equity rather than debt. Point them to the company's own disclosure to the exchanges, which states the objects of the issue, rather than to market commentary. On the selling question, do not advise them either way, because that is a personal investment decision and you are not a registered adviser. Do flag two practical things: the trading window and insider trading code may restrict when employees can transact, especially around a fundraise, so they must check with compliance first, and a decision driven by a 3% move in one morning is rarely a considered one.

body.title: How to Read an IPO Document Without a Finance Degree
steps: Find the objects of the issue and read exactly what the fresh money will be used for, watching for vague headings like general corporate purposes
Check the split between fresh issue and offer for sale, so you know how much reaches the company
Read the first five risk factors, since companies list the most material ones prominently
Look at who is selling and how much, because a promoter exiting a large stake at listing is worth understanding
Check the basis for the issue price section, which sets out the valuation logic and peer comparison
Scan related party transactions and any pending litigation involving the promoters

cards.definition: Draft Red Herring Prospectus: the first public disclosure document filed with SEBI before an IPO, covering business, financials and risks.
Red Herring Prospectus: the near-final version filed with the price band and issue dates, before bidding opens.
New shares created and sold, with the money going to the company.
Existing shareholders selling their shares, with the money going to them rather than to the company.
A large institutional investor allotted shares before the issue opens, subject to a lock-in, whose participation signals institutional interest.
Application Supported by Blocked Amount: your application money is blocked in your bank account rather than debited, until allotment.
Qualified Institutional Buyer: mutual funds, insurers, banks, pension funds and foreign portfolio investors.
The tradable right to subscribe to a rights issue, which existing shareholders can use or sell on the exchange.
Theoretical ex-rights price: the blended price a share should settle at once discounted rights shares are issued.

body.label: SEBI: Public Issue Filings
body.description: Draft offer documents for upcoming IPOs are published on SEBI's site under filings. If your employer, a customer or a competitor is going public, the DRHP is the most detailed public description of that business you will ever get.

points: Equity can be raised through an IPO, an FPO, a QIP, a rights issue or a preferential allotment, and each has a different investor base and timeline
Only fresh issue money reaches the company; an offer for sale pays the selling shareholder instead, and most Indian IPOs combine both
SEBI reviews IPO disclosure, it does not certify that the price is fair, and the final price is discovered through bidding within a band
A QIP is the fast route for listed companies, open only to institutions, with pricing anchored to recent market prices
A rights issue is offered to existing shareholders at a discount, and the theoretical ex-rights price shows why that discount is not free money
Ignoring a rights issue is the worst option, because entitlements can usually be sold on the exchange instead
Dilution is only bad if the capital raised earns less than it costs, so the question to ask is what the money buys

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice or a recommendation to participate in any issue. Allocation percentages, timelines and procedural rules are set by SEBI regulations that change from time to time, so verify current requirements in the offer document and on SEBI's website. All figures used are illustrative.
